title: Can I Start a Side Hustle While Employed Full Time? 7 Checks
meta_description: Can I start a side hustle while employed full time? Often, yes. Check these 7 clauses and policies first, then tell your employer the right way.
quick_answer: Often, yes. You can legally start a side hustle while employed full time in many places, but your employment contract, company policies and local law set the limits. Check for outside-activity, conflict-of-interest, IP assignment, non-compete, non-solicit and confidentiality terms. Then use only personal devices and time, avoid your employer's clients and competitors, get written approval if required, and ask an employment lawyer if unsure.
key_takeaways: You can often start a side hustle while employed full time, but your contract, company policies and local law set the limits.
Before you start, check seven areas: outside-activity, conflict-of-interest, IP assignment, non-compete, non-solicit, confidentiality and equipment-use rules.
Broad IP clauses can cover work you do at home, so get a written carve-out that names your project before you put serious time into it.
Stay out of your employer's market. Don't take its clients, prospects, suppliers or competitors as customers, and don't recruit coworkers.
Use only personal devices, accounts and hours, and tell your employer in writing when your contract requires it.
Rules vary by country, state and industry. If your idea is close to your day job, speak to an employment lawyer where you live.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for full-time employees who want to freelance, sell products or build something on the side without risking their job or their ownership of what they create.
intro: You have a skill, an idea or a product you want to sell, and a full-time job you want to keep. Often you can do both. What's allowed for you depends on documents you probably signed and forgot about. This guide shows you which clauses to look for in your contract and company policies. It also gives you a ready-to-use email for telling your manager or HR, shows how to keep your side hustle fully separate from your job, and explains how to fit it around a full-time schedule without your job performance slipping. This is general information, not legal advice. Rules vary by country, state and industry.

steps.name: Gather every document you signed
steps.text: Collect your employment contract, offer letter, employee handbook, code of conduct, IT and social media policies, and any invention, confidentiality, equity or bonus agreements. Download the current policy versions from your HR portal, because policies may have changed since you joined.

steps.name: Search for the key clauses
steps.text: Search each document (Ctrl+F or Cmd+F) for 'outside', 'other business', 'conflict', 'invention', 'intellectual property', 'compete', 'solicit', 'confidential' and 'acceptable use'. For each match, note the document name, clause number and exact wording. Headings can be misleading, so read the clause itself.

steps.name: Rate your idea against each clause
steps.text: For each clause, ask whether your side hustle overlaps with your employer's products, customers, suppliers or competitors, or with the skills you're paid to use. Mark it green (no overlap), amber (some overlap) or red (direct overlap). If anything is amber or red, slow down and get clarity before you start.

steps.name: Check local law and special rules
steps.text: Look up how your country or state treats non-competes and employee inventions, using official government guidance where you can. Also check rules from your industry or regulator, public-sector codes, and any work-visa conditions that limit other work, including self-employment.

steps.name: Decide whether to tell your employer
steps.text: If your contract requires notice or approval, you must tell your employer before you start. If it says nothing but your idea scored amber or red in step 3, telling your employer is usually the safer choice.

steps.name: Disclose in writing and keep the answer
steps.text: Use your company's disclosure form if it has one. If not, email your manager or HR with a short description that shows there's no conflict (a template is in the section on telling your manager or HR). Ask for a written reply, and record the date and the name of the person who approved it.

steps.name: Separate everything before you start
steps.text: Before you do any side-hustle work, set up a personal device, a separate email address, a payment account and a bank account. Decide now that you won't take on your employer's clients, prospects, suppliers or competitors, however small the job.

steps.name: Set a schedule you can keep up
steps.text: Choose a weekly limit on hours that you could keep up even in a busy month, and block those hours in your personal calendar outside paid time. Tell clients your availability up front so you never feel you have to reply during work hours.

steps.name: Keep records and review regularly
steps.text: Keep a dated log of your side-hustle work and separate financial records. Check the rules again when you change roles, sign new documents, your employer updates its policies or your side hustle changes direction.

sections.heading: Can I Start a Side Hustle While Employed Full Time? The Short Answer
paragraphs: Often, yes. In many countries it's legal to run a side hustle while employed full time, but your employment contract, your employer's policies and local law decide what you can actually do.

The law itself rarely stops employees from earning money outside work. The limits usually come from what you've agreed to, such as a clause requiring approval for outside work, a conflict-of-interest policy or an IP clause. Local law then decides how far those clauses can be enforced, and that differs between countries and even between US states.

These rules are rarely all in one place. Check your contract and offer letter, employee handbook, code of conduct, IT and social media policies, and any separate invention, confidentiality, equity or bonus agreements. Use the current versions on your HR portal.

Some people face stricter rules from the start. Public-sector employees, people in regulated fields such as financial services, healthcare or law, and anyone on a work visa tied to one employer should check those rules before taking on any outside work.
The risk levels below give you a quick first read on your idea.
bullets: Lower risk: unrelated to your employer's business and done on your own time and equipment, such as a software engineer selling handmade furniture at weekends.
Medium risk: the same skills in a different market, such as an in-house marketer writing blog posts for local restaurants. Read the IP and conflict-of-interest wording closely.
Higher risk: the same industry or similar customers, such as an agency designer freelancing for the kind of small businesses the agency pitches to.
Highest risk: working for a competitor, serving your employer's clients, or using company time, equipment or information.

sections.heading: Moonlighting and Conflict-of-Interest Rules
paragraphs: Moonlighting (or outside-activity) clauses decide whether you can do other paid work at all, and conflict-of-interest policies decide which kinds of work are off-limits.

Outside-activity clauses usually take one of the four forms below, and the exact wording matters more than the heading. Check whether approval has to be in writing, who can give it, and whether the clause says your employer can't refuse consent without good reason.

Read the definitions too. Some clauses cover unpaid roles, company directorships or shareholdings as well as paid work. That means even registering a company or advising a friend's startup might need to be disclosed.

Conflict-of-interest policies cover situations where your personal interests could clash with your employer's. Examples include working for a competitor, supplier or customer, using your role to win business for yourself, or owning a stake in a company you deal with at work. An unrelated side hustle rarely triggers these policies, but the closer it gets to your day job, the more likely it is to.

Even without a written clause, the law in many countries expects employees to act in good faith toward their employer. This is often called a duty of loyalty or fidelity. Competing with your employer while you're still on its payroll is risky almost everywhere.
Also look for wording that asks you to give your 'full working time and attention' to the job. If your performance slips, that can cause problems even when the side hustle itself is allowed.
bullets: Outright ban: no other paid work or business. Whether it can be enforced depends on local law, but breaking it can still put your job at risk.
Approval required: you need permission before you start, ideally in writing.
Notice only: you have to tell the company, but you don't need its permission.
No clause: conflict-of-interest, confidentiality and IP rules still apply.

sections.heading: IP Assignment Clauses: Who Owns What You Build on Your Own Time
paragraphs: An IP assignment clause can give your employer ownership of what you create. Some are broad enough to cover work you do at home on your own equipment.

In many countries, employers own the work you create as part of your job by default, and the IP clause sets out how much further that goes. Narrow clauses cover only work done 'in the course of' your employment. Broad clauses can cover anything 'related to the company's business or anticipated research', or anything you create 'during' your employment, no matter where or when you made it.

This matters most if your side hustle involves software, apps, designs, courses, writing or inventions. Unclear ownership tends to come up at the worst moment, for example when a buyer, investor or partner asks you to confirm that you own what you're selling.

Some places limit how far these clauses can reach. Several US states, including California, stop employers from claiming inventions you develop entirely on your own time without company equipment, supplies, facilities or trade secrets. These protections generally don't cover inventions that relate to your employer's business or research, or that come from work you did for your employer. Other countries have their own rules.

If your project is close to your employer's field, ask for a written exception (a carve-out) before you put serious time in. For example: 'Please confirm that [Company] claims no ownership of [project name], a [one-line description] I'm developing on my own time and equipment, under clause [X] of my employment agreement.' If you're signing a new contract, list your existing projects on any prior-inventions list it includes.
bullets: Does the clause say 'in the course of employment' (narrower) or 'during employment' (broader)?
Does it mention work 'related to' the business or its 'anticipated research'?
Is there a prior-inventions list, and did you fill it in when you joined?
Do you have to report new inventions or creations to the company?

sections.heading: Non-Compete, Non-Solicit and Confidentiality Terms
paragraphs: Non-compete clauses limit competing with your employer, non-solicit clauses limit approaching its clients or staff, and confidentiality terms limit using its information. All three can affect a side hustle.

Non-competes can apply while you work there, after you leave, or both. Whether they can be enforced varies widely. Some places restrict or ban them for many workers, while others enforce them if they're reasonable in length, area and scope. The rules have changed in several places in recent years, so check current local law before assuming a clause can't be enforced.

Non-solicit clauses are often the biggest practical risk. They usually stop you approaching your employer's customers for your own benefit, and some also cover prospects and colleagues. Watch for 'non-dealing' wording, which can stop you working with a client even if the client contacts you first.

The simplest protection is to stay out of your employer's market entirely. Don't take on its clients, prospects, suppliers or direct competitors as customers, and don't recruit coworkers as partners or contractors without checking your contract first.

Confidentiality duties usually apply whether or not your contract spells them out. Pricing, client lists, internal templates, processes, code and unreleased plans belong to your employer, and rebuilding them from memory can still count as a breach. Never paste work material into personal AI tools or side-hustle documents.
bullets: How long does any non-compete last, and which activities and places does it cover?
Does the non-solicit cover only clients you dealt with, or all clients and prospects?
Does it stop you hiring or working with coworkers?
How does the contract define confidential information?

sections.heading: How to Tell Your Manager or HR About Your Side Hustle
paragraphs: The safest way to raise a side hustle is in writing, after you've read the relevant policies, with a short description that shows there's no conflict.

If your contract requires notice or approval, you have to tell your employer, and staying quiet is usually the bigger risk. If your contract says nothing, telling them is still often sensible when your side hustle is close to your field. The three approaches below keep the conversation low-key.

Share just enough to show there's no overlap: what the side hustle is, roughly how much time it takes, and that you'll use your own equipment. You don't need to share a business plan or how much you earn.

Sample email. Subject: Outside activity – quick policy check. 'Hi [Name], I'd like to be upfront about a small outside project I'm planning: [one line, e.g. weekend portrait photography for private clients]. It's unrelated to [Company]'s products and customers. I'll do it outside working hours on my own equipment and accounts, and it won't use any company information or involve colleagues. I've read [policy name] and don't believe it creates a conflict, but I'd appreciate your confirmation in writing. If there's a form I should use instead, please let me know. Thanks, [Your name].'

Ask for a written reply, and record the date and the name of the person who approved it. Check your IT policy before forwarding work email to a personal account. If forwarding isn't allowed, note the details in your personal log instead.

If the answer is no or comes with conditions, ask what would make it acceptable, such as a different niche, excluding certain clients, or a date to review the decision. Then decide whether to adjust the idea, wait or drop it.
bullets: Use the formal process: if your company has a disclosure form for outside activities or conflicts of interest, fill it in. It's designed for this and creates a clear record.
Ask HR a neutral question first, such as 'What's the process for disclosing an outside activity?' That way you learn the steps before sharing any details.
Mention it in a regular one-to-one with your manager, then confirm by email. That gives you both the conversation and a written record.

sections.heading: Keep Your Side Hustle Separate From Your Day Job
paragraphs: The best everyday protection is a clear line between your job and your side hustle: separate devices, accounts, hours, customers and money.

Using a work laptop, phone, email address, software licence or office network for side-hustle tasks can break IT policy and strengthen your employer's claim to what you build. It can also expose your plans, because many companies monitor their systems. Watch for less obvious overlaps too. Signing into your personal browser profile on a work laptop can sync your side-hustle files and passwords onto a company device.
Keep a simple dated log, on your own devices, of when and where you worked on your project. It won't guarantee anything, but it can help show you built it independently if questions come up.
bullets: Devices: use your own laptop and phone, and keep files in a personal cloud account, never on the company drive.
Accounts: set up a separate email address, payment account and bank account. Never sign up for tools with your work email.
Hours: work outside paid time. An unpaid lunch break on your own phone is usually fine, but be especially strict if you work remotely, because blurred hours are easy to question.
Customers and information: no clients, prospects or competitors of your employer, and nothing from work, including templates, contacts, pricing or code.
Public profile: don't suggest your employer endorses your side hustle, and check the social media policy before listing your services on LinkedIn.
Money and tax: track side income and expenses separately, set some money aside for tax, and check your local rules, because side income is usually taxable.

sections.heading: Fitting a Side Hustle Around a Full-Time Job
paragraphs: A side hustle fits around a full-time job when you plan for your energy as well as your hours, because slipping at your day job can cost you more than the side hustle earns.

Start with a weekly limit on hours that you could keep up in a busy month, not just a quiet one. Block those hours in your personal calendar the way you would a meeting, and treat anything beyond them as optional. The sample week below is a starting point, not a target.

Some side hustles fit around office hours better than others. Work you can do in your own time, such as writing, design, editing, digital products or bookkeeping for clients who don't compete with your employer, is easier to schedule than work that needs daytime calls or same-day replies.

Set client expectations from day one. State your availability, for example 'evenings and weekends, replies within one working day', in your proposals. Use an auto-reply on your side-hustle email, and turn off side-hustle notifications during work hours so you're not tempted to reply on company time.
Automate repetitive admin, such as order confirmations, form submissions and invoices, so the business keeps running while you're at work. Keep every connected account personal.
Review your routine every month. If you're missing day-job deadlines, taking side-hustle calls at work or running on empty, cut your hours or pause new clients before your manager notices.
bullets: Two weekday evenings: focused client or product work.
One weekend block: bigger tasks, content or product development.
One short slot: admin, invoicing and replies.
At least one evening with no side-hustle work at all.

sections.heading: When to Get Advice From an Employment Lawyer
paragraphs: Get advice from an employment lawyer if your contract is unclear, your side hustle overlaps with your employer's business, or you've been asked to sign something new.

Employment rules vary by country, state and industry, and the same clause can be enforceable in one place and not in another. A short consultation can cost far less than sorting out a dispute over who owns your business later.

To keep the meeting focused, bring your contract, the relevant policies, any written approvals and a one-paragraph description of your side hustle. Depending on where you live, unions, professional bodies and free legal advice services may also offer employment guidance.
bullets: Your side hustle is in the same industry, uses the skills you're paid for, or could attract similar customers.
Your contract has a broad IP or invention clause, and you're building software, products or content to sell.
You've been asked to sign a new contract, policy acknowledgement or invention agreement.
Your employer has refused permission or raised a concern.
You're on a work visa, work in the public sector, or work in a regulated profession.

recommendations.best_for: A private workspace on a personal account and device where you keep side-hustle notes, track tasks, keep a dated log of your work and store copies of written approvals. The built-in AI can help draft and summarise your own documents.
recommendations.not_for: Anyone tempted to use their employer's Notion workspace or work login, or to paste company information into it. It may also be more than you need if a simple notes app already works. Check current plans and AI features on Notion's site.

recommendations.best_for: Side hustlers with regular income and expenses who want separate books, invoicing and automatically sorted transactions. It keeps side-hustle money apart from personal finances and makes tax time easier.
recommendations.not_for: Very small or occasional side income, where a simple spreadsheet may be enough. It doesn't replace an accountant's advice on your local tax rules. Check current plans and prices on the vendor's site.

recommendations.best_for: Busy employees who want routine side-hustle admin to run automatically while they're at their day job, with no code. Examples include logging new orders or form submissions, sending confirmation emails or creating invoices. It connects thousands of apps.
recommendations.not_for: Anyone who would connect it to work accounts or company tools, so keep every connected app personal. If you expect to run a high volume of automations, compare it with Make, which can cost less at scale. Check current plans and integrations on Zapier's site.

recommendations.best_for: Side hustlers running an online store who get customer questions during the workday. Live chat plus an AI support agent can answer routine questions such as shipping and returns, so you can deal with the rest after work instead of on company time.
recommendations.not_for: Service-based freelancers or stores with little traffic, where an email inbox and a clear FAQ page are enough. Check AI answers before relying on them, and confirm current plans and store integrations on Tidio's site.

faq.question: Do I have to tell my employer about my side hustle?
faq.answer: It depends on your contract and company policies. If they require notice or approval for outside work, tell your employer before you start, because not doing so can lead to disciplinary action. If they say nothing, you may not be legally required to tell them, but it's often wise when your side hustle is close to your day job.

faq.question: Can I get fired for having a side hustle?
faq.answer: Possibly, depending on where you work and what your contract says. In most US states employment is at-will, which lets employers dismiss staff for almost any lawful reason. Many other countries require a fair reason and process. Breaking a clear moonlighting, conflict-of-interest or confidentiality rule makes dismissal much more likely, so read the rules first.

faq.question: Does my employer own what I create on my own time?
faq.answer: Not automatically, but it might. Ownership depends on your IP assignment clause and local law, and broad clauses can cover work related to your employer's business even if you did it at home. Using company equipment or information strengthens your employer's claim, so keep side projects completely separate and get any exception in writing.

faq.question: Can I freelance in the same field as my day job?
faq.answer: Sometimes, but it's the riskiest kind of side hustle. Work in the same field is more likely to trigger conflict-of-interest, non-compete, non-solicit and IP clauses. If you go ahead, avoid your employer's clients, prospects and competitors, get approval in writing, and consider advice from an employment lawyer.

faq.question: Can I start an LLC or limited company while employed full time?
faq.answer: In many places, employment law doesn't stop you registering a business, but your contract still applies to whatever that business does. Some outside-activity policies specifically cover directorships or owning a business, so check whether registering a company is something you must disclose. Don't use your work address, email or phone in the registration.

faq.question: Do I need to pay tax on side hustle income?
faq.answer: Generally, yes. Side hustle income is usually taxable and often has to be reported even when it's small. Rules on thresholds, registration and payment deadlines vary by country and state, so set some money aside and check your local tax authority's guidance or speak to an accountant.

conclusion: You can often start a side hustle while employed full time, but the first step is reading your paperwork, not finding customers. Check your contract and policies for the seven clauses and policies in the table above, rate your idea against each one, and tell your employer in writing when your contract requires it or your idea is close to your field. Keep everything on personal devices, accounts and hours, stay out of your employer's market, and set a schedule you can keep up. If anything is unclear, talk to an employment lawyer where you live before you put serious time or money into the idea.
